title: Pull a jammed card out of a printer with both hands
instruction: Clear the paper jam and resume printing.
context: Clearing a paper jam is one of the most familiar printer chores at home and in the office: every printer maker's manual has a section on it, and anyone who prints meets it sooner or later. Media torn while it is pulled out leaves scraps in the paper path that cause the next jam. Canon's manual for its GX5000 home printers gives the procedure for paper jammed in the feed slot of the rear tray: "Hold jammed paper firmly with both hands and pull it out slowly. Slowly pull out the paper so as not to tear it." Then: "Press printer's OK button. The printer resumes printing." The instruction only says to clear the jam and resume printing. Here a card is jammed and the two feed rollers, visible at the slot's mouth, grip it near both edges: pulled up by one edge, or by its middle, it skews in the slot and tears beside a roller. Clearing the jam takes both arms pulling it straight up together, one above each roller.
setup: A table in front of two arms (bases 61 cm apart), seen by one overhead camera and a camera on each wrist. Positions are in cm from the midpoint between the two arm bases: x forward (away from the arms), y to the robot's left. A black portable inkjet printer (x 22 to 40, y -15 to 15, 7 cm tall) stands with its back toward the arms. A printed white DL card (21 x 9.9 cm, fed landscape) has jammed in the feed slot of its rear tray (x 24.0 to 24.6, y -10.6 to 10.6, 5 cm deep): it stands in the slot with its top 5 cm sticking out, and two light grey feed rollers at the slot's mouth (y 5 to 10 and -10 to -5) press it against the slot's wall near both edges. The OK button (1.6 cm across) is on the printer's top at x 31, y -11. The printer is fixed; the card is loose. Real trial: the card is 300 g/m2 card stock, about 0.4 mm thick (the simulation's card is a 3 mm rigid stand-in, see fidelity); to set the jam, feed it landscape into the rear tray's slot, start a print and switch the printer off as the rollers draw it in, with its top 5 cm out; a light pull on one corner must not free it. The layout is the same in every trial, as in the screenshot.
scoring: The bodies' poses are read from the simulation, and each gripper's centre from the arm's joints. The card is three strips joined along two seams; a seam shears when one side is pulled harder than the other, and once a seam has sheared 1.5 mm or more the card has torn: 0 for the rest of the run. Otherwise partial credit is the best stage reached: 0.25 the card raised 1.5 cm or more; 0.5 out of the printer (its bottom edge above the printer's top); 0.75 put down on the table in front of the printer (at rest, no gripper holding it). 1.0: that, with the OK button pressed after the card came out, both grippers 6 cm or more from the card and the button, still for 1 s. Doing nothing scores 0. With a real printer, whether the card came out whole is judged from the card itself and from the videos.
reset_notes: Put the card back in the feed slot as in the screenshot (standing on the slot's floor, its top 5 cm out, gripped by both rollers). In the simulation each trial starts the simulator afresh (each inspect-robots run does).
fidelity: Rigid bodies in Isaac Sim 6.1 (PhysX), 20 Hz control. The printer is the size of a portable inkjet printer. The real card is 300 g/m2 card stock about 0.4 mm thick, which bends; the simulation's card is a 3 mm rigid stand-in that does not bend: three rigid strips whose two seams slide up and down on a 1 N/mm spring; a seam sheared 1.5 mm counts as torn. Each feed roller presses the card with about 4 N. The printer does not print: pressing OK stands for resuming printing.
scores: Dream-1 run: 0.0 (both arms reached over the printer and the right gripper came down beside the card's right end, but neither gripper took the card, which stayed jammed); demo: 1.0
